title: Purpura: the differential diagnosis
summary: Not every purple spot is vasculitis. Sort purpura into flat (platelets, clotting, fragile vessels) and palpable (vasculitis), and look for the dangerous causes: sepsis, leukaemia, DIC and systemic vasculitis.

glance.think: Non-blanching red or purple spots or bruises, in a child or an adult.
glance.engine: Low or faulty platelets, clotting problems, fragile vessels (age, steroids, scurvy) or vessel inflammation.
glance.backbone: Glass test; is the patient unwell? FBC and film, clotting, U&E, LFT, CRP, urine; same-day if unwell or platelets low.
glance.never_miss: Meningococcal sepsis, leukaemia, ITP, DIC, cryoglobulinaemic or ANCA vasculitis, non-accidental injury.

what: Short comparison cards for the four other options and the emergency that must always be excluded.

cause.h: How they are caused / 8.3 Clinical features

head: Condition
Mechanism
Who / features
rows: **Infants 4 months–2 years**: large **rosette/target/medallion purpuric plaques** on face, ears and limbs with oedema and fever, but **the child looks well**. Usually skin-only; resolves in 1–3 weeks
Cold-precipitating immunoglobulins (type II/III mixed — **hepatitis C**, Sjögren's, lymphoma; type I — myeloma/Waldenström's occlusion)
Adults; palpable purpura on legs, **acral necrosis/ulcers, livedo**, Raynaud's, arthralgia, neuropathy, **membranoproliferative GN**, low C4; DIF IgM ( option 5)

Rare in children; sinusitis, crusting, epistaxis, saddle nose, lung nodules/haemorrhage, **GN**; skin: palpable purpura, ulcers, nodules, **oral ulcers/"strawberry gums"**. Biopsy: **necrotising vasculitis with granulomas** ( option 2)
Autoantibody platelet destruction (often post-viral in children)
**Well child, flat petechiae and bruising, mucosal bleeding; platelets <100 (often <20) × 10⁹/L**; otherwise normal FBC/film. Most children recover in 6 months
*N. meningitidis* endotoxin → DIC and septic vasculitis

**Unwell, febrile child or young adult**; rapidly spreading **non-blanching petechiae → purpura fulminans**; cold peripheries, leg pain, abnormal colour, tachycardia, ± neck stiffness — a **999 emergency**

diagnosis: FBC + film (platelets), clotting/D-dimer/fibrinogen (DIC), blood cultures/meningococcal PCR, ANCA, cryoglobulins (37 °C), HCV, C3/C4, urinalysis.
differentials: Also: non-accidental injury, Henoch–Schönlein purpura (see *IgA vasculitis*), leukaemia, haemophilia/von Willebrand, scurvy, HUS, drug-induced thrombocytopenia (heparin, quinine, valproate, co-trimoxazole).
management: **NICE NG240:** in suspected meningococcal disease, transfer immediately to hospital; give **parenteral benzylpenicillin** (or ceftriaxone/cefotaxime) at the earliest opportunity **if it will not delay transfer**. Doses: benzylpenicillin IM/IV — **adults and children ≥10 years 1.2 g; 1–9 years 600 mg; <1 year 300 mg** (check BNF/BNFC). Many community IP settings will not hold it — call 999.
Any non-blanching rash in an unwell or febrile patient → 999. Purpura + low platelets → same-day haematology. Purpura + sinus/lung/renal symptoms or positive ANCA → urgent rheumatology/renal.
red_flags: Unwell with a non-blanching rash: **999**, benzylpenicillin if there will be a delay (NICE NG240).
Petechiae with pallor, lymph nodes, bone pain or bruising: **same-day FBC and film** (leukaemia, ITP).
pearls: Teach parents the **glass/tumbler test**, but stress that an **unwell child needs urgent help even if the rash blanches**.
